# PostMortem AI — full reference

Canonical product: [https://www.nanoneuron.ai/](https://www.nanoneuron.ai/)

[GitHub outage demo](https://www.nanoneuron.ai/blog/github-outage-demo) (the tool's own unedited output on a real public incident)

Contact: vish.matale@gmail.com
Last factual review: 2026-09-13

This file is the complete reference; llms.txt above is the short index. Every
claim here is checked against the running code and, where practical, against
live production behavior as of the review date — not a roadmap or an
aspirational description. If this file and the running product ever disagree,
the running product is correct and this file is stale.

## What this is

A single-account incident postmortem tool for DevOps and SRE teams, and for
freelance SRE/DevOps consultants working a single client engagement: record
evidence about an incident as it unfolds, generate an AI-drafted postmortem
grounded in that evidence, publish it once a named human approves. Each
account is one person's own incidents — no shared organizations, teams, or
roles yet, so a freelancer serving multiple clients is one account per
engagement today, not built-in multi-client management.

## Architecture

- Backend: FastAPI (Python), deployed as a Vercel serverless function.
- Frontend: Next.js App Router (React), deployed to Vercel.
- Database: PostgreSQL (Supabase), accessed via a connection pool; pooled
  (`:6543`) connections disable server-side prepared statements to avoid a
  transaction-pooler incompatibility.
- AI: Gemini (`gemini-2.5-flash` by default for drafting/extraction,
  configurable via `GEMINI_MODEL`; `gemini-embedding-001`
  for RAG embeddings at 768 dimensions, matching the `vector(768)` column).
  Claude is a real, configured fallback provider (not just described), used
  only when Gemini's own call fails or its circuit breaker is open — each
  provider has its own independent circuit breaker (closed/open/half-open).
- 29 forward-only SQL migrations as of this review.

## The core guarantee: grounded drafting

Two independent layers, not one unsupervised model call:

1. The drafting model receives the incident's evidence entries, numbered, and
   is instructed (system prompt, verbatim rules): every claim must cite an
   entry number; an unsupported section should be left empty/uncited rather
   than inferred; never estimate cost, revenue, or customer counts not stated
   in the evidence; never invent dates, deadlines, or names; never recommend
   an action the evidence doesn't support; retrieved similar past incidents
   (RAG, below) are reference-only and must never be cited.
2. Code — not a second model call — independently re-verifies every citation
   against the real evidence list before anything is persisted. An invalid
   citation (missing, out of range, wrong type) causes that claim to be
   replaced with the fixed marker `"Not established by the recorded
   evidence."` for the four required sections (summary, root_cause,
   detection, resolution), or dropped entirely for optional lists
   (contributing_factors, actions). This step can only remove or replace the
   model's own text — it has no path to add new text of its own.

Verified live, deliberately adversarially, not just on the happy path: a
draft built from genuinely vague evidence ("things felt slow... got better
later") correctly returned the literal `root_cause` marker rather than
inventing a cause, and every other field stayed strictly within the vague
language actually given — no fabricated numbers, dates, or causes. Drafting
with zero evidence entries is refused outright (409) rather than attempted.

Publishing requires a named human approval; `incident_postmortems` has a
database `CHECK` constraint that a row cannot be marked `published` without
both `approved_by` and `approved_at` set — enforced at the schema level, not
just by application code or a UI convention.

## RAG (similar past incidents)

When drafting, the account's own previously *published* postmortems that are
semantically similar to the current incident are retrieved via cosine
similarity over embeddings and shown to the model as labeled reference
context — never numbered, never citable. The citation-verification step only
ever checks against the current incident's own numbered evidence, so a
retrieved past incident structurally cannot become the source for a claim,
regardless of what the model outputs.

## Drafting style (per-account tuning, in context)

`GET/PUT/DELETE /v1/postmortems/preferences` (session) holds the account's
house style: up to 1,500 characters of instructions on phrasing and
structure, plus whether the account's most recent approved, published
postmortem is shown to the drafting model as an example of how the team
writes (on by default, switchable). Both are appended to the system prompt
(`SYSTEM_PROMPT` v4, rule 7) — never to the numbered evidence — and govern
form only: a style instruction cannot add a fact and the example is never
citable; `ground_draft` still drops every uncited claim. Drafts made with a
style record `prompt_version = "v4+style"` on `ai_runs` and the postmortem
row. There is no weight tuning and no training on customer content; see
`docs/FINE_TUNING.md`.

## Evidence model

Each evidence entry has: `source` (a fixed type category — `alert`, `log`,
`deploy`, `metric`, `human_note`, or `customer_report`; not a vendor/tool
name), `summary` (required), `detail` (optional), `occurred_at` (epoch
milliseconds), and is attributed to whoever/whatever recorded it (a signed-in
user, or `"webhook"` for automated ingestion). Incidents have a `severity` of
`sev1`–`sev4` and a `status` of `open`/`resolved`.

## Webhook ingestion

Every account has a real, rotatable per-account token
(`GET /v1/webhooks/token`, `POST /v1/webhooks/token/rotate` — rotating
immediately invalidates every URL built with the old token). Posting to
`/v1/webhooks/incidents/{token}` either appends to an existing open incident
(if `incident_id` is given and belongs to the caller) or creates a new one —
the same write path and paywall as the authenticated app, just authenticated
by token instead of session cookie. Rate-limited to 100 events/hour per
account. Generic, source-agnostic — put the sending tool's name in
`summary`/`detail`. An optional `resolved: true` on an event appending to
an existing incident auto-transitions it to resolved, matching the
resolved-event most real monitoring tools already send — one-directional
only (never reopens a resolved incident) and only takes effect when
appending to an existing incident, never on creation.

`POST /v1/webhooks/pagerduty/{token}` is a second, PagerDuty-specific
adapter over the same underlying write path (both routes share one
`_ingest_event()` — the paywall check, rate limit, and evidence insert are
never duplicated). It parses PagerDuty's real v3 webhook envelope
(`event.event_type`, `event.data.id/title/urgency/html_url`) directly:
`incident.triggered` creates an incident and stores PagerDuty's own
incident id as `incidents.external_id` (migration 0025); a later
`incident.resolved` for the same PagerDuty incident id finds that same
row by `external_id` and resolves it, since PagerDuty has no way to be
told this app's own incident id back. Urgency (`high`/`low`, PagerDuty's
only two levels) maps conservatively to `sev2`/`sev4`. Any other event
type gets a 200 with `{"status": "ignored"}` rather than an error —
PagerDuty disables a subscription after enough non-2xx responses, and
there's no per-event-type filter in its own subscription config.
Datadog has no adapter route: its webhook payload is entirely
user-templated on Datadog's side, so its "integration" is a documented
JSON template (account settings) for Datadog's own webhook payload field,
pointed at the generic endpoint above — there is no fixed Datadog schema
to parse.

`POST /v1/webhooks/slack/{token}` is a Slack Events API receiver over the
same `_ingest_event()` write path — paste it as a Slack app's Event
Subscriptions Request URL, subscribe to `message.channels`, invite the app
to an incident channel, and the channel records itself as the incident
unfolds instead of being pasted in afterwards. **A Slack thread maps to one
incident**: `external_id` is `slack:{channel}:{thread_root_ts}`, so the
first message opens an incident and every reply appends evidence to that
same one, via the identical `external_id` lookup PagerDuty uses. A message
outside a thread keys on its own `ts`, so unrelated channel chatter is
never absorbed into someone else's incident. Slack's one-time
`url_verification` challenge is answered before the token lookup, since it
carries no account context.

Three refusals in that route are deliberate, not omissions. **Bot messages
are dropped** — this app posts its own notifications *into* Slack via the
outbound `slack_webhook_url` integration, so ingesting bot output would feed
those back as evidence and the product would cite text it wrote itself.
**Edits and deletions are ignored** (`message_changed`, `message_deleted`) —
evidence is append-only and provenance-preserving, so a later edit must not
rewrite a row already cited. **Nothing auto-resolves from chat** — someone
typing "we're resolved" is not an authenticated state change, unlike a
PagerDuty resolve, which is a real transition in a system of record and does
auto-draft. Evidence lands with `source: human_note`, one of the six values
`incident_evidence`'s CHECK constraint permits. Unrecognised payloads return
an ignored 200, since Slack disables a subscription that keeps failing.
Authentication is the URL token only, like the other webhook routes.

## Similar-incident retrieval, evidence quality, and draft comparison

`GET /incidents/{id}/similar` runs the same account-scoped, published-only
similarity search drafting already uses internally as hidden RAG context,
reachable directly so a human can see "3 incidents like this before" ahead
of drafting, not just have it invisibly shape the model's output.
`GET /quality-summary` aggregates how often each of the four required
sections came back as the fixed unsupported marker across the account's
own drafts — a pattern-level signal about evidence habits, not a
judgment on any single draft. `GET /incidents/{id}/previous-draft`
returns the snapshot taken immediately before the most recent re-draft
overwrote it (`postmortem_draft_history`, append-only), so a re-draft is
comparable to what it replaced instead of an unexplained rewrite.

## MCP

The backend exposes a real MCP server (`/mcp` on the API; federated to
`/api/mcp` on the frontend under the caller's own session), 15 tools
total: founder-only (`get_founder_summary`, `list_payment_claims`,
`approve_payment_claim`, `reject_payment_claim`, `run_read_only_sql` — a
defense-in-depth read-only query tool, `list_agent_activity` — the
cross-account activity-log query below) and client-scoped
(`list_incidents`, `get_dashboard_summary`, `create_incident`,
`add_evidence`, `draft_postmortem`, `find_similar_incidents`,
`publish_postmortem`, `get_integrations`, `update_integrations`) — the
same business logic and authorization as the REST endpoints below, not a
parallel implementation.

## Agent accountability

Every MCP tool call is recorded into `account_activity_log` (the same
table REST-driven actions already wrote into, tagged `source='web'` vs.
`source='mcp_agent'`), including denials: a `PermissionError` raised by
one of the three subscription/founder gates above is caught and logged as
a denial before propagating, so a blocked attempt is visible, not just a
successful one. Reads and writes are split into an explicit command
(`RecordActivityCommand`/`handle_record_activity`) and query
(`ActivityLogFilter`/`handle_activity_log_query`, real keyset pagination
on `(created_at, id)`, not `OFFSET`) in `app/cqrs/activity.py`, shared by
every reader: `GET /v1/postmortems/activity-log` (caller's own account),
`GET /v1/founder/activity-log` (every account, filterable by
client_email/source/time window), and the `list_agent_activity` MCP tool
above -- one query implementation behind all three, not three that could
drift apart.

## REST API surface (all under `/v1`)

Airlock (`/v1/airlock`): `POST /scan` (paid; authenticated by an API key in
`X-Airlock-Key` or `Authorization: Bearer alk_...`, or by the dashboard
session cookie; spends 1 prepaid credit, or 5 with `"deep": true`; scores
content for prompt injection and returns verdict, score, matched rule ids
with their descriptions, the normalisation signals, `credits_remaining`,
`credits_charged` and -- on a deep scan -- the Gemini opinion; 401 without
a key or session, 402 with nothing scanned when the balance is short),
`POST /egress` (paid, same authentication, 1 credit; checks an outbound
payload and destination, returns the payload redacted), `GET /pricing`
(public; pack size and price per currency, credits per scan and per deep
scan, which manual rail takes each currency), `GET /stats` (public;
aggregate counts and the most-fired rules -- no content, ever),
`POST/GET /keys` and `DELETE /keys/{id}` (session; mint a key -- the secret
is returned once and only its SHA-256 is stored -- list, revoke),
`GET /credits` (session; balance, totals, and a statement rolled up per
key per day), `POST /credits/claim` (session; "I have paid for N packs in
this currency, here is the reference" -- amount and credit count are
server-derived, lands as a pending payment claim the founder approves),
`GET /credits/claims`, `POST /credits/email-details` (session; the payee
details for a pack, sent to the caller's own registered address),
`POST /waitlist` (public; records early-access interest in a self-hosted
build, answers 202 identically whether
the address is new or already on the list so the response cannot be used to
enumerate it), `GET /waitlist` (founder-only; the list itself).

Auth (`/v1/auth`): `POST /register`, `POST /login`, `POST /logout`,
`GET /me`, `PUT /me`, `PATCH /me`, `DELETE /me` (founder account cannot
self-delete), `POST /password-reset/request`, `POST /password-reset/confirm`,
`GET /captcha-config`, `GET /session-token`.

Incidents & postmortems (`/v1/postmortems`): `POST /incidents/suggest`
(AI-suggested title + severity from pasted raw text, for the create form to
pre-fill -- suggestion only, creates nothing), `POST /incidents`,
`GET /incidents`, `GET /incidents/{id}`, `PATCH /incidents/{id}/status`,
`GET /summary`, `POST /incidents/{id}/evidence`,
`GET /incidents/{id}/evidence`, `POST /incidents/{id}/evidence/extract`
(AI-assisted extraction from pasted raw text), `POST /incidents/{id}/draft`,
`POST /incidents/{id}/publish`, `PATCH /incidents/{id}/public`,
`GET /incidents/{id}/postmortem.md` (the postmortem as a Markdown file in the
same shape as /postmortem-template: evidence numbered, every citation
resolved to a number, the dropped-claim count included),
`PATCH /incidents/{id}/actions/{action_id}` (follow-up tracking: move a
drafted action item through open / in_progress / done / dropped; `GET
/summary` reports `open_actions` still owed across all incidents),
`GET /public` (list published+public postmortems), `GET /public/{slug}`,
`GET /export` (the caller's own full data as JSON), `GET /activity-log`
(the caller's own account_activity_log rows, source-tagged web vs.
mcp_agent -- see Agent accountability above).

Billing (`/v1/billing`): `GET /status`,
`GET /upi/pricing` (public), `GET /upi/info` (founder-only — the real UPI
ID is never returned in an API response to a client account),
`POST /upi/email-details` (self-serve: emails the real UPI ID to the
caller's own registered address, no founder round-trip needed),
`POST /upi/claim`, `GET /upi/claims`, `GET /wire/pricing` (public),
`GET /wire/info` (founder-only, same reasoning as UPI),
`POST /wire/email-details` (self-serve, same as UPI above),
`POST /wire/claim`, `GET /wire/claims`, `PATCH /claims/{id}` (edit a
still-pending claim's reference), `DELETE /claims/{id}` (withdraw a
still-pending claim), `POST /bank-alert` (inbound webhook for a forwarded
real bank credit alert — verifies a claim's reference against a real bank
alert but never itself grants access; only a founder's explicit approval
does that).

Webhooks (`/v1/webhooks`): `GET /token`, `POST /token/rotate`,
`POST /incidents/{token}`.

Integrations (`/v1/integrations`): `GET ""`, `PUT ""` (Slack webhook URL,
Linear API key/team ID — best-effort notifications on publish, never block
the publish response on failure).

Founder-only (`/v1/founder`): `GET /summary`, `GET /payment-claims`,
`POST /payment-claims/{id}/approve`, `POST /payment-claims/{id}/reject`,
`POST /payment-claims/{id}/annotate`, `GET /payment-claims/{id}/events`,
`GET /activity-log` (every account's activity, not just the caller's own
— filterable by `client_email`, `source`, `since_ms`/`until_ms`, keyset
`cursor`-paginated; see Agent accountability above).

## Auth model

Session cookie, HMAC-signed. `current_user` (401 if absent/invalid) vs
`current_founder` (403 if signed in but not the configured founder email) are
distinct dependencies — a request with no session gets 401; a real, signed-in
non-founder account hitting a founder-only route gets 403. Login is
rate-limited per account and per IP; registration and password-reset requests
are separately rate-limited by IP; drafting and incident creation are
rate-limited per account (the AI-cost-incurring actions). Registration/login
can require a Cloudflare Turnstile CAPTCHA when configured. Login and
password-reset both give an identical, generic failure message regardless of
whether the account exists — deliberately, to prevent account enumeration.

## Payments

Creating an incident, evidence, AI extraction, drafting, publishing, and
creating a second incident all require an active subscription.

**Price.** One plan, no tiers. India: ₹999/month or ₹9,990/year via UPI.
International: USD 15, GBP 12, or EUR 14 per month, or USD 150, GBP 120, or
EUR 140 per year, via SWIFT wire. Annual is charged for ten months, so two
months are free (`ANNUAL_MONTHS_CHARGED`, default 10). Live prices are served
publicly and unauthenticated from `GET /v1/billing/upi/pricing`
(`amount_inr`, `amount_inr_annual`) and `GET /v1/billing/wire/pricing`
(per-currency `amount`, `amount_annual`) — those endpoints, not this
document, are the authority if the two ever disagree.

**Annual is the recommended option for international customers, and not as a
discount.** A SWIFT wire costs the sender roughly USD 15–40 in bank fees.
Against a USD 15 monthly subscription that is a surcharge larger than the
product itself, every month, so monthly-by-wire is not economically sensible;
annual makes it a one-off cost on a single larger transfer. The billing
period is stored on the claim (`payment_claims.billing_period`, migration
0029, constrained to `monthly`/`annual`) rather than inferred from the
amount, because an amount alone is ambiguous across currencies and approval
needs to know unambiguously how long a grant should last.

For clients in any country, two real paths work today: (1)
manual UPI (India), founder-reviewed; (2) manual international SWIFT wire
(USD/GBP/EUR), founder-reviewed. Both are self-serve to get started: a
signed-in client requests the real account details (UPI ID; wire account
number, SWIFT code, correspondent bank) via `POST /upi/email-details` or
`POST /wire/email-details`, which emails them to that client's own
registered address -- no founder round-trip needed just to find out how
to pay. Submitting the transaction reference afterward still requires the
founder's explicit approval before access activates. Indian-diaspora customers are not limited to wire: an NRI with an
NRE/NRO account and an international mobile number (US, UK, Canada,
Australia, Singapore, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Oman, Malaysia,
Hong Kong, France) can pay via UPI in INR instead, instantly and
with none of the correspondent-bank fees a wire incurs. The wire
payment-details email says so explicitly.
There is no third path: the card-processor integration that used to
exist was removed on 2026-09-13 on the owner's decision, so UPI and wire
are the only rails and nothing renews unless the customer pays again.
Manual claims are matched to real bank alerts
automatically (verification only — a founder's explicit approval is the only
thing that ever activates access, regardless of automated verification).
Every real payment endpoint verifies against the provider's own record
(amount, currency, signature, captured status), never against
frontend-supplied state.

**There is no free tier and no trial.** Every incident, from the first,
requires an active subscription. The gate is enforced in one place
(`has_free_incident_available` in `apps/api/app/auth.py`, permanently False)
and honoured identically by the REST API, the MCP tools and the webhook
ingestion path, so it cannot be bypassed by choosing a different entry point.
History: the one-free-incident trial was switched off on 2026-09-04, restored
on 2026-09-10 on funnel evidence, and retired again on 2026-09-13 by the
founder's explicit decision. Accounts that already held a free incident from
before keep working on that one incident (never publishing it, never a second)
-- a promise the site made them at the time is kept. To judge the output
before paying, read https://www.nanoneuron.ai/blog/github-outage-demo, a full
postmortem the tool drafted from a real public outage; the 14-day refund on
the first charge is the safety net. Every payment claim has a printable
document at /invoice/{claim id} (session-gated, never indexed): a proforma
invoice while pending -- what a finance team needs to raise a wire -- and a
receipt once the founder has verified the payment, with the amount, the
reference and the verification date; the confirmation and approval emails
link to it. The seller block comes from SELLER_LEGAL_NAME / SELLER_ADDRESS /
SELLER_TAX_ID (falling back to the bank beneficiary name). An account that signed up at least a
day ago and has never paid for either product (no subscription, no payment
claim in any state, no Airlock credits) receives exactly one automated
reminder email, ever: the worked example, the prices, and how to pay from
any country — never a repeat send and never a fabricated urgency claim.
Accounts with a payment claim in flight are excluded on purpose.
Refunds: email vish.matale@gmail.com within 14 days of the first charge
and it's refunded — a manual, founder-processed action on every payment
rail, the same review discipline as approving a payment in the first
place. No self-serve automated refund endpoint exists — deliberately:
this app's whole identity is that consequential actions need a human,
not inferred approval, and an automated outbound-money action would be
the same thing in reverse.

## What this doesn't do

- Auto-publish anything — always a deliberate, named human action.
- Estimate cost, revenue, or customer-impact figures the evidence didn't
  state — the system prompt explicitly forbids it.
- Vendor-specific webhook parsing beyond PagerDuty (real adapter) and
  Datadog (documented payload template) — any other monitoring tool
  still works via the generic, un-adapted webhook endpoint.
- Support multiple people, teams, or roles on one account.
- Claim any measured quality score, uptime percentage, or customer count
  that hasn't actually been measured — this file states architecture and
  verified behavior, not marketing figures.

## Access & discovery

Public marketing/docs/published-postmortem pages are meant to be indexed;
every account-scoped page requires authentication and is not meant to be
crawled as public data. No API keys, credentials, or account-specific data
are ever exposed in this file or any public page.

## Airlock (main product)

Airlock is a paid guard that sits between an AI agent and untrusted
content. Two directions:

- **Inbound.** Text is normalised first -- Unicode tag-block characters
  decoded, invisible characters stripped, HTML comments and hidden elements
  extracted, spaced-out obfuscation collapsed -- then scored against 40
  weighted rules across 8 attack families (instruction override, role
  hijack, delimiter break, exfiltration, tool abuse, authority spoof, memory
  poison, encoding). Scores combine with noisy-OR rather than addition, so
  several weak signals cannot sum to false certainty. Block at 0.75, flag at
  0.40 by default; each account can set its own thresholds and mute rules
  (policy, below). With `"sanitize": true` the response also carries a
  `sanitized` copy of the content with hidden characters, hidden HTML and
  the strongest matches removed, at no extra charge.
- **Outbound.** Destination checked against an allowlist (the call's list
  merged with the account policy's standing list); payload checked
  against 11 credential patterns (AWS access key and secret, Anthropic,
  OpenAI, GitHub, Slack, Google, Stripe, private keys, JWTs, bearer tokens)
  and 7 personal-data patterns (email, E.164 phone, credit card, SSN,
  Aadhaar, PAN, IBAN), plus a query-string entropy check.

Audit: one append-only entry per decision, holding a SHA-256 of the scanned
content, its byte count, the verdict and the rules that fired. The raw
content is never stored, and the hosted scanner stores no excerpt either.
Rows carry no account, key or IP, deliberately: an append-only table cannot
take part in an account erasure, so it holds nothing about a person to
erase. Attribution and metering live in a separate credit ledger (migration
0032) that cascades with the account.

Append-only is enforced by two Postgres triggers (migration 0031) -- a
row-level one rejecting UPDATE and DELETE, and a statement-level one
rejecting TRUNCATE. The second is not redundant: TRUNCATE fires no row-level
trigger, and was verified to empty the table silently before it was added.

By default there is no model call and no network request in the decision
path, so the scanner has no undecided state; a failure inside the
application is a 5xx that carries `"verdict": "block"` in its body and no
charge -- the guard fails closed, and a client that reads the body before
the status agrees with one that does not. (A platform failure before the
application runs returns the platform's own error page, which is why the
rule for callers is "any non-200 is a block".) Policy, usage and the CSV
export are not metered but are bounded per account: 600 reads and 60
exports an hour, then 429 with Retry-After. `GET /v1/airlock/stats` returns public aggregates only; the
customer's own usage is at `GET /v1/airlock/usage` (per day, per key) and
`GET /v1/airlock/usage.csv` (every ledger line), both drawn from the credit
ledger, never the audit log, because the audit log has no account column.

**Proxy fetch (`POST /v1/airlock/proxy/fetch`, 2 credits).** The agent
gives Airlock the URL instead of fetching it: the URL is checked as an
outbound call (policy allowlist merged with the call's; credential material
in the query string blocks), then fetched from Airlock's own address under
a server-side request forgery guard (app/airlock/proxy.py): every address
the host resolves to is checked -- loopback, private, link-local (cloud
metadata), CGNAT, reserved, multicast, unspecified, documentation ranges,
IPv4-mapped and NAT64-embedded IPv6 all refuse, decimal/hex/short IPv4
literals are recognised before DNS, and a name resolving to a mix of public
and private addresses is refused; the connection is pinned to the checked
address with the hostname as Host and TLS server name (so rebinding between
check and connect cannot land the request elsewhere, and the certificate is
still verified against the real name); redirects are followed by hand and
re-checked, at most 3; bodies are read to 1 MB; only text types are
scanned; nothing of the caller's (headers, cookies) is forwarded. The page
is scanned under the account policy (script/style stripped, hidden elements
and comments kept for the normaliser) and the visible text is returned on
allow, sanitized on flag, null on block; `stage` says whether the egress
check or the ingress scan decided. A URL that will never be fetched is 422,
an unreachable public URL is 502; both refund the scan credit, keep one
credit for the attempt (a refused fetch is never a free probe of what
resolves where), and carry `"verdict": "block"`. An application error
after any charge refunds that charge on the ledger. Deep scan adds 4 credits, refunded when the rules
already block.

**Writing and feeds.** /blog lists every post (worked examples on real
public outages, and how the grounding mechanism works); /feed.xml is the
RSS 2.0 feed of the same posts. /airlock/benchmark is the benchmark's own
page with every miss verbatim; /airlock keeps the summary. Guessed URLs
(/airlock/pricing, /airlock/docs, /docs/airlock, /rss.xml) redirect to
where the thing lives.

**Fine-tuning (status, honestly).** The only model-behaviour layer in either
product is Airlock's deep-scan classifier. A fine-tuning dataset builder
(apps/api/scripts/airlock_finetune_dataset.py: 718 rows from the public
benchmark set and the self-authored corpus -- never customer content;
574 train / 144 held-out, stratified, seeded) and an evaluation harness for
the current classifier on the held-out split
(scripts/airlock_semantic_eval.py) exist and are tested; the held-out split
and manifest are committed. No deep-scan number has been published yet
(the harness needs a valid Gemini key and refuses to write a result when
every call fails), and no weights have been tuned (gemini-2.5-flash tuning
needs Vertex AI billing this company does not currently have). Full
account: docs/FINE_TUNING.md. PostMortem AI has no fine-tuning by design:
its guarantee is enforced by code after the model answers, and its only
possible training material is customer data the privacy policy excludes.

**Rule pages.** Every detection rule has its own page at
https://www.nanoneuron.ai/airlock/rules/<id lower-cased> (index at
/airlock/rules): what it catches, its weight and what that weight means
under noisy-OR, its family, its language (the 1xx series is German), how
many injections it fired on in the public benchmark, and how to mute it
for an account. Generated at build time from apps/web/app/airlock/rules.json,
which a test pins to apps/api/app/airlock/rules.py; the patterns are never
published there.

**SDKs.** Official clients in the repository under sdk/python (package
`nanoneuron-airlock`, `from airlock import Airlock` / `AsyncAirlock`; httpx
only) and sdk/typescript (package `nanoneuron-airlock`, `new Airlock({ apiKey
})`; zero dependencies). Methods: scan, egress, fetch, policy, usage, rules.
Every non-200 raises/throws a typed error (AuthenticationError 401,
InsufficientCredits 402, RateLimited 429 with retry_after, FetchRefused for
a proxy 422/502, AirlockError otherwise) carrying the request id; nothing
is retried. Both are tested in CI against the real in-process API (Python)
and a recording fetch (TypeScript). Not yet published to PyPI/npm as of this
file's date; install from the repository path.

**Conditional GET.** GET /v1/airlock/rules and /v1/airlock/pricing carry an
ETag; send it back as If-None-Match and get a 304 with no body. Every
metered route's request body ships an example in the OpenAPI document, and
the X-Request-ID, Server-Timing and Retry-After headers are declared there.

**Policy (per account, migration 0034).** `GET /v1/airlock/policy` (key or
session) returns `block_threshold`, `flag_threshold`, `muted_rules` and
`egress_allowlist`; `PUT` replaces it and `DELETE` resets it, from a
signed-in session only. A key can read the policy it runs under and cannot
change it, so a leaked key cannot raise the block threshold and switch the
guard off. Muted rules are skipped before their pattern runs; the policy
row is fetched in the same query as the key, so a keyed scan pays no extra
round trip. Every scan response names the policy applied. The rule
vocabulary (id, family, weight, description; not the patterns) is public
at `GET /v1/airlock/rules`.

**Deep scan (opt-in per call, `"deep": true`, 5 credits).** After the rules
run, the same Gemini provider that drafts postmortems (app/airlock/
semantic.py) classifies the content and its answer enters the same noisy-OR
as one more weighted term, capped at 0.85 -- below the strongest single
rule. It can only raise a verdict, never lower one: its weight is zero
unless it says "injection". When the rules alone already block, the model
is not asked (it could not change anything): the five credits are taken up
front as for any deep scan -- the paywall stays in front of the engine --
then four are refunded as a ledger line, and the response says
`semantic.status: "skipped"` with `credits_charged: 1`. There is deliberately no lower bound: the paraphrased attack
that scores 0.00 on rules is the case the second opinion exists for. If
Gemini is unavailable or answers unparseably, the response says
`semantic.status: "unavailable"`, the rule verdict stands, and the 4 extra
credits are refunded as a ledger line. A
deep scan sends the content to Google's Gemini API; the audit row still
holds only the hash. The classifier's contribution is recorded as rule id
`AI-001`.

**Tuning (customer feedback loop).** A wrong verdict is reported with
`POST /v1/airlock/feedback` (not metered): the scan's `content_sha256`, the
verdict given, the verdict expected and the rule ids. `GET /v1/airlock/tuning`
returns the account's reports and what they add up to -- a rule reported as
a false positive on three distinct scans becomes a "mute this rule"
suggestion applied in one call (`POST /v1/airlock/tuning/mute`, session
only, through the account policy); two reported misses from one source
become a "send deep: true for this source" suggestion. A report may include
`content`; only then is the text stored, and then it does two things: it is
shown to Gemini as a worked answer on that account's deep scans (the eight
most recent, in-context, weights untouched, `semantic.examples` says how
many), and it exports as `GET /v1/airlock/tuning/export.jsonl` in the same
Vertex AI supervised-tuning format the repository's own dataset builder
writes. Reports are withdrawable (`DELETE /v1/airlock/feedback/{id}`) and go
with the account. The founder sees per-rule false-positive counts across
accounts -- never content -- which is the signal for reweighting a rule in
`rules.py`, benchmarked before it ships. No customer content trains any
model. Full account: `docs/FINE_TUNING.md`.

**Pricing and metering.** Airlock is paid and has no free tier. Prepaid
packs of 10,000 scan credits: INR 999 by UPI, or USD 15 / GBP 12 / EUR 14 by
international SWIFT wire, up to 10 packs per payment; one credit per scan or
egress check, five per deep scan; credits do not expire. Buying is a
payment claim on the same manual rails as the PostMortem AI subscription:
the customer has the payee details emailed to their own address, pays,
submits the transaction reference, and the founder approves it from the
dashboard -- approval is what grants the credits, in the same transaction
that marks the claim approved. The debit is a conditional UPDATE on a
balance row with `CHECK (balance >= 0)`, so concurrent scans cannot
double-spend (tested: 50 concurrent scans against 10 credits yield exactly
10 successes and 40 402s). There is no card processor. The founder's
own account is the only one not metered.

**API contract.** The OpenAPI document at
https://postmortem-ai-api.vercel.app/openapi.json (interactive at /docs)
declares the three authentication schemes (X-Airlock-Key header, Bearer,
session cookie), documents 401/402/422/429 on the metered routes, carries
clean operationIds (`scan`, `egress`, `create_key`, `submit_pack_claim`)
for generated clients, and names the production server. Every response
carries `X-Request-ID` (a caller-supplied id is echoed) and `Server-Timing`
(app-side duration); a 500 body includes the same request id. Responses
over 1 KB are gzip-compressed when accepted. `/v1/airlock/pricing` and
`/stats` are the only cacheable responses; everything authenticated is
`private, no-store`. Every 429 carries `Retry-After`. The customer is
emailed once when the balance first drops below 1,000 credits and once
when it reaches zero (stateless: sent on the call that crosses the line).

**Where to read more.** The human-readable API reference is the first
section of https://www.nanoneuron.ai/docs#airlock; /status shows the
Airlock API's reachability, app-side latency and region, re-checked every
30 seconds; the counters on /airlock refresh from /v1/airlock/stats every
minute; the dashboard's Airlock panel re-reads balance, keys and claims
every 20 seconds while open.

**Geography and language.** The API is global (HTTPS from anywhere, no
region restriction) and model-agnostic. Payment from any country by SWIFT
wire in USD/GBP/EUR, or by UPI within India -- the only rails. The 30
rules match English phrasing; the deep scan classifies content in any
language. Outbound patterns cover international formats (E.164 phone,
IBAN, card, email) plus US SSN and Indian Aadhaar/PAN.

**Status, stated precisely because it is the thing most likely to be
misreported.** Two halves, and they differ:

RUNNING NOW -- the detection engine, the egress check, proxy fetch (the
SSRF-guarded URL retrieval above), the Gemini deep scan, sanitize-on-request, the append-only audit log, API keys (hashed,
revocable), prepaid credits with an atomic per-call meter, a per-account
policy (thresholds, muted rules, standing egress allowlist), the public
rule list, usage by day and key with CSV export, a readable ledger, pack
purchase via UPI/wire claims, fail-closed 5xx bodies, the tuning feedback
loop (reports, suggestions, in-context tuned deep scans, JSONL export), and
the dashboard to buy, mint, revoke and tune -- all served from this site's own FastAPI
backend under `/v1/airlock`. The playground at
https://www.nanoneuron.ai/airlock calls the real endpoint from the
signed-in account's credits.

NOT BUILT -- proxy forward (Airlock sending an outbound call on the
caller's behalf with credentials stripped), alert webhooks, any
support or uptime commitment, and a self-hosted build; the early-access
list on that page is for the self-hosted build only. NOT PLANNED -- a free
plan or trial (every scan is paid, including the first), and any card
processor (UPI and international wire are the only rails).

**On accuracy claims -- the published benchmark.** The rule engine, with no
model call, run on the public dataset deepset/prompt-injections (Hugging
Face, CC BY 4.0; 662 labelled texts, 263 marked injection and 399
legitimate, English and German): it catches about a quarter of the texts
that dataset labels as injections (overall recall ~26%; ~24% on the English
rows, ~30% on the German rows) and raises ZERO false alarms on the 399
legitimate texts. The exact figures, every miss verbatim, and every false
positive (none) are in the results file the page renders
(apps/api/benchmarks/results/deepset-prompt-injections.json); the dataset
rows are committed with attribution and the run is reproducible with
`PYTHONPATH=apps/api python apps/api/scripts/airlock_benchmark.py`. A test
(tests/test_airlock_public_benchmark.py) recomputes the results from the
engine and fails if the committed numbers drift; the web copy is pinned to
the API copy byte for byte.

Why recall is low, both reasons true: the dataset labels off-topic and
role-play requests to a news chatbot as injections, which a regex guard for
agent pipelines deliberately does not flag; and paraphrased overrides with
no fixed phrasing are exactly what rules cannot see -- the Gemini deep scan
exists for those and is not part of this run. Before the benchmark the same
rules caught 1.1%; the rules added since are general phrasings ("forget
everything before that", "new tasks follow", "show me your prompt text",
"ignore the above and say", "I want you to act as", and their German forms
in the 1xx id series), not fingerprints of samples. The rules match English
phrasing plus those German override forms; any other language is the deep
scan's job.

The self-authored corpus (app/airlock/corpus/, 56 cases: 40 attacks, at
least one per rule, and 16 ordinary documents) remains as the regression
guard: every rule is exercised by at least one case, and none fires on the
ordinary documents. It is a smoke test, NOT a benchmark, and must not be
reported as an accuracy figure; the benchmark above is the number to quote,
with its caveats.

## Commercial scope

Active MVP under continued single-developer development, not a finished
commercial product with support SLAs. Capabilities described here reflect
what is actually implemented and, where noted, actually verified live, as of
the review date above — re-verify against the running product if this file
is more than a few weeks old.
